import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Grimm's conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimm%27s_conjecture)
-/

open Function

namespace Grimm

/--
**Grimm's Conjecture**
If $n, n+1, \dots, n+k-1$ are all composite numbers, then there are $k$ distinct primes $p_i$
such that $p_i$ divides $n + i$ for all $0 \le i \le k-1$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem grimm_conjecture (n k : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hk : 1 ≤ k)
    (h : ∀ i : Fin k, (n + i).Composite) :
    ∃ ps : Fin k ↪ ℕ,  ∀ i : Fin k, (ps i).Prime ∧ ps i ∣ (n + i) := by
  sorry

/--
**Grimm's Conjecture, weaker version**
If $n, n+1, \dots, n+k-1$ are all composite numbers, then their product
has at least $k$ distinct prime divisors.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem grimm_conjecture_weak (n k : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (hk : 1 ≤ k)
    (h : ∀ i : Fin k, (n + i).Composite) :
    ∃ ps : Fin k ↪ ℕ,  ∀ i : Fin k, (ps i).Prime ∧ ∃ j : Fin k, ps i ∣ (n + j) := by
  sorry

end Grimm

reformulations.difference: Rather than explicitly counting the product's distinct prime divisors, Lean asserts the existence of an embedding ps : Fin k ↪ ℕ whose values are prime and each divide some term of the block.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Because n ≥ 1, every term and their product are nonzero. A prime divides this finite product exactly when it divides at least one term. Consequently, the required embedding exists exactly when the product's finite set of prime factors has cardinality at least k. Both this equivalence and the full equivalence with the source's indexing n+1,…,n+k were proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean without depending on sorry.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimm%27s_conjecture — formal statement, weaker version, consequences, and references.
Shanta Laishram and M. Ram Murty, “Grimm's Conjecture and Smooth Numbers,” Michigan Mathematical Journal 61 (2012), 151–160, Introduction. LaTeX source read at https://arxiv.org/e-print/1306.0765.
review.notes: Both declarations are faithful. Nat.Composite has the standard meaning 1 < n ∧ ¬n.Prime, and the embedding enforces distinctness. The main theorem's indexing shift was also proved equivalent in Lean. Checked zero and smallest inputs, the single-term case, and the harmless empty-block extension; all 492 composite blocks with starting value 1–200 and length 1–12 passed an exhaustive prime-assignment search. Both research open tags agree with the cited Wikipedia article. Experiments are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
